content: Segesterone acetate and ethinyl estradiol are indicated for use in females of reproductive potential to prevent pregnancy. Before initiating the vaginal system, it is important to consider the possibility of ovulation and conception. The vaginal system should be inserted into the vagina and remain in place continuously for 21 days (three complete weeks). After this period, the system should be removed for a one-week dose-free interval, during which withdrawal bleeding typically occurs. Following the dose-free interval, the same vaginal system, after being cleaned, should be reinserted for another 21 days. This cycle of three weeks in and one week out provides contraception for 13 cycles. To insert the vaginal system, users should wash their hands thoroughly and choose a comfortable position, such as lying down, squatting, or standing. The sides of the vaginal system should be pressed together for insertion into the vagina. When properly inserted, the system should be entirely within the vagina and positioned behind the pelvic bone. The efficacy of this contraceptive method is expected to be similar in post-pubertal adolescents under 18 years of age and users aged 18 years and older. However, it is not indicated for use before menarche. Certain medications, such as belzutifan, mavacamten, omaveloxolone, carbamazepine, and others, can decrease the effectiveness of segesterone/ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic or intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. In such cases, alternative or additional nonhormonal contraceptive methods should be used. Additionally, some drugs, like levoketoconazole, may increase hormone levels, requiring close monitoring. Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of serious cardiovascular events in females using combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs), particularly in those over 35 years of age. CHCs should not be used by females older than 35 who smoke. The risk of arterial or venous thrombotic diseases is higher in females with a history of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, cerebrovascular disease, coronary artery disease, or other thrombotic conditions. CHCs are contraindicated in females with uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes with vascular complications, or a history of estrogenor progestin-sensitive cancers. Females with a history of depression should be carefully monitored, and CHC use should be discontinued if depression worsens. Similarly, new or worsening headaches, particularly migraines, should prompt evaluation and possible discontinuation of the vaginal system. Females with hypertriglyceridemia or a family history of the condition may be at increased risk of pancreatitis when using CHCs. Additionally, CHCs may exacerbate gallbladder disease or cholestasis in susceptible individuals. The estrogen component of the vaginal system may increase serum levels of certain binding globulins, potentially necessitating dose adjustments for thyroid or cortisol replacement therapy. In females with hereditary angioedema, exogenous estrogens may trigger or worsen symptoms. Cases of toxic shock syndrome (TSS) have been reported in vaginal ring users, though a causal relationship has not been established. If TSS is suspected, the vaginal system should be removed, and appropriate medical evaluation and treatment should be initiated. Epidemiologic studies have not shown an increased risk of birth defects with CHC use before conception or during early pregnancy, but the vaginal system should be discontinued if pregnancy occurs. CHCs can reduce milk production in breastfeeding females, particularly during the early stages of lactation. Nursing females should consider alternative contraceptive methods until breastfeeding is discontinued.
